reconcile.connective: Commentators harmonize by distinguishing the price required (100) from the price David actually paid (200), with Clarke instead arguing the original text read 100 throughout.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, who lists the passage in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses the two figures as a self-disagreement of the text, though he grants David may simply have paid twice the asking price.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: he mentions but one hundred, though he gave two hundred as her dowry, no more being required than one hundred; see Sa1 18:25.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles 200 (1 Sam 18:27) with 100 (2 Sam 3:14): David paid 200 but cites the 100 that was the actual required price.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The number was doubled, partly to show his respect and attachment to the princess, and partly to oblige Saul to the fulfilment of his pledge.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explains the 200 as a deliberate doubling of the 100 required, so the two numbers reflect required vs. delivered, not a contradiction.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The Septuagint has only one hundred men. Saul covenanted with David for a hundred; and David himself says, Sa2 3:14, that he espoused Michal for a hundred: hence it is likely that one hundred is the true reading.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Text-critical reconciliation: the LXX reads 100 and agrees with 2 Sam 3:14, so the 200 in the MT is treated as a scribal corruption of an originally consistent 100.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on 2 Samuel 3:14
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats the passage directly, harmonizing the figures: David paid two hundred as the dowry but cites the one hundred Saul actually required.
